<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-grounded cases without fake precision, and both suffered one clipped turn. PRO's best weapon—the trap that CON admitted the short-lived roofer "pays under both policies"—was pressed consistently, but CON met it head-on with the strongest weighing in the debate: the roofer pays in different currencies, a structured wage fraction that can be loaded onto high earners versus retirement years that are "one hundred percent of what pensions promised him." CON also answered PRO's pressure questions honestly (conceding legislated age rises can be defensible while defending progressive taxation as the main instrument, which keeps CON on the motion as written), and landed two damaging turns PRO never fully neutralized: the labor-market laundering point (an age hike that pushes unhirable elders onto disability converts a pension promise into the exact cost-shifting PRO condemned) and the "no failure threshold means faith, not policy" hit, which PRO's symmetry reply only partially defused. PRO's responses were competent but more repetitive, centered on the years-paid/years-drawn ratio without new comparative work late. CON's closing crystallized the clash more decisively ("which currency do you collect it in?"), giving B a clear but competitive edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.3–B4.5: CON's "different currencies" rebuttal reversed PRO's strongest trap—conceding the roofer pays under both policies but arguing a wage deduction borne by the lawyer's full income is categorically cheaper than confiscating the only retirement years the roofer would ever collect—then compounded it by turning PRO's own condemnation of cost-shifting against his disability answer and his missing failure threshold.</best_rebuttal>
